overview: Wartime OWI inquiry and State's reply on Kwantung's status: Japan administered the leased territory, but China retained sovereignty, and the US never recognized Manchukuo.

people.name: John Herrick
people.role: Chief, Washington Bureau, Culpeper Branch, Office of War Information

people.name: Paul M. Hancock
people.role: Member of the Media Analysis and Language Research Department, Office of War Information

subfiles.title: State Department reply on the status of the Kwantung Leased Territory
subfiles.from: Robert E. Hull, Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.to: John Herrick, Office of War Information
subfiles.about: The State Department explains the United States’ position on the lease, sovereignty, and administration of the Kwantung Leased Territory.
subfiles.summary: State tells OWI that treating Japan as Kwantung's administering authority didn't abandon China's sovereignty, and rejects claims the territory was incorporated into Manchukuo.

subfiles.title: Office of War Information request for clarification of Kwantung policy
subfiles.from: Paul M. Hancock, Media Analysis and Language Research Department, Office of War Information
subfiles.to: U.S. Department of State, Division of Current Information
subfiles.about: Hancock asks whether the United States recognized the 1915 extension of Japan’s lease and how it regarded the territory’s legal status.
subfiles.summary: OWI's Hancock asks whether the US recognized the 1915 lease extension or considered Kwantung part of Manchukuo.

interest: Shows how the US distinguished recognizing Japan's administration from recognizing sovereignty over Kwantung.
